structure.title: 7. Welfare effects and incidence of licensing (structural estimation)
8. Why are some occupations licensed but not others?

observations.statement: The design is named a two-way fixed-effect comparison of state-occupation cells with high versus low licensed shares relative to both the occupation and the state; the estimand is described as an average treatment effect for occupations with interstate policy disagreement, a policy-relevant margin.

The identifying assumption is written formally: two-way differences in cell licensed shares across any pair of occupations and states must be independent of the corresponding two-way differences in cell-average errors. The intro gives an informal version using example occupation-state pairs.
observations.locator: Section 4, equation (10) and displayed independence condition
observations.quote: highly licensed state-occupation cells are otherwise comparable to cells with lower licensed rates

observations.statement: The estimator is rewritten as a weighted average of heterogeneous cell-level effects following de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille; the share of negative weights is reported in a footnote and an appendix table ranks occupations by weight. The authors state what homogeneity is required (within occupation across states, not across occupations).

A dedicated section lists four threats: validity of the licensed share as a policy proxy, confounding labour-market institutions, spillovers (SUTVA), and selection on worker heterogeneity. Each gets its own subsection with a check.

The authors discuss the political-economy origins of within-occupation interstate policy variation, admit they do not fully understand them, and point to appendix tests using partisan self-identification data.

Data are the public basic monthly CPS via IPUMS over a stated four-year window, using the new licensing questions; the unit is the worker, with the treatment measured at the state-occupation cell (2010 Census occupation codes).

The main sample excludes universally licensed occupations (per an external list) to reduce measurement error, and the authors note results with them included appear in appendix tables. Employed adults in a stated age band are kept, except age regressions.
observations.locator: Section 3, Section 4, footnote 14, Appendix Tables A9 and A11

observations.statement: Every regression table panel reports observations and the number of clusters; table notes explain why sample sizes fluctuate across robustness columns (controls unavailable or cells dropping out).

A hand-collected cell-level dataset of actual licensing policies for a subset of occupations (where definitions align and data are available) is used to validate the survey proxy; the list and collection procedure are in appendices.
observations.locator: Section 3, footnote 16, Appendix D, Appendix Table A5

observations.statement: Licensed status is defined from two survey questions (active credential and government-issued), following the BLS convention; a footnote explains why the third question (required for job) is not used. Certification is defined separately and used as a control.

The cell licensed share is a leave-out mean shrunk toward the occupation's national share with a beta-binomial empirical Bayes adjustment; a posterior standard deviation per cell is computed to quantify attenuation from sampling variance. Formulas are given in the main text.

Misreporting bias is assessed by looking at occupations with known licensing status, and a simple rescaling correction is described but not applied; the authors state the net direction of sampling and misreporting biases and leave estimates unadjusted.

Outcomes are log hourly wage (MORG sample), log weekly hours, years of education, worker age, and log cell employment counts; earnings top-coding and allocation follow Autor et al., with winsorization of low earnings and of very high weekly hours, and education mapped to years.

Controls enter as fixed effects for demographic strata built from characteristics the authors argue are predetermined with respect to licensing; a narrower control set is used for the human-capital outcomes because education is itself an outcome.

The main table has three columns per outcome panel: individual licence status with controls, cell share without controls, cell share with controls (the baseline). Notes list the fixed effects, the cluster level, the restriction to a common sample, and pointers to appendix variants.

Outcomes are stacked as panels within one table (education, age, wage, hours, employment), with the employment panel estimated at the cell level and reported in a single column since worker-level controls are not meaningful there.
Weighting is stated only in the structural table notes: earnings weights for the MORG sample and final weights for the non-MORG sample. Employment counts are described as sample-weighted.
Regression tables do not report R-squared or the mean of the dependent variable; a within-R2 for a control regression is mentioned only in a footnote.
Standard errors are clustered at the state-occupation cell, the level at which the treatment (licensed share) is defined; this is stated in the design section and repeated in every table note.
observations.quote: We cluster standard errors by cell, which we define to be a state-occupation pair.

observations.statement: The choice of cell over state clustering is justified by a variance decomposition showing state-level averages explain little variation; an appendix table reports that state clustering leaves standard errors unchanged.
For the log-count employment regression, a Poisson specification is reported in the appendix and framed as a check that OLS on log counts is not biased by heteroskedasticity.
observations.locator: Section 5.3, Appendix Table A8 Panel B

observations.statement: The treatment proxy is validated two ways: comparing self-reported licensed rates between universally licensed and other occupations, and regressing the cell share on hand-collected policy indicators in the two-way FE specification, with a residualized binned plot in the appendix.
observations.locator: Section 3, Appendix Table A6, Appendix Figure A4

observations.statement: An appendix table decomposes licensed-share variance into between-occupation, state, and residual components, and the residual share is presented explicitly as the identifying variation; its dispersion feeds an attenuation calculation.
The main linear relationships are re-estimated semiparametrically in an appendix figure, referenced from the main table notes.
For the structural model, an appendix robustness check calibrates two more parameters so the system is overidentified and reports tests of the overidentifying restrictions.

Model-predicted employment responses by mobility quartile are compared with estimated responses and a test of equality is reported in a footnote, serving as an out-of-sample validation of the model's selection mechanism.

An IV variant instruments the licensed share with indicators for cells whose residual share is more than one SD above or below zero, argued to isolate policy-like variation and purge suboccupation demand and sampling noise; reported as Column 1 of the robustness table.

One robustness table with five columns spans all outcome panels: IV, certification and union controls, PCA plus Bartik-like predicted-employment controls, state by occupation-group FE, and division by occupation FE. Each column is motivated in text by a named threat.
The employment analysis is repeated using ACS microdata for outcomes while keeping the CPS-based licensing measure, presented as a self-replication that rules out common-source bias.

Structural robustness is done by re-running the minimum distance estimator on each column of the reduced-form robustness table; the authors state which structural estimates are sensitive and which conclusions survive.
A bounding approach to selection on unobservables following Oster is mentioned as an appendix exercise.

Two unidentified structural parameters are calibrated from cited literature ranges and the structural table reports nine columns varying each across a grid, with the text noting which estimates are invariant to calibration and a footnote giving the constructive identification argument.

Selection is probed by splitting workers into quartiles of demographic-stratum occupational transition rates, re-estimating each outcome per quartile, and reporting a test of equality between extreme quartiles in a fifth column.

Occupation-level heterogeneity in the WTP effect is modelled as a correlated random coefficients regression with a quadratic in the national leave-state-out licensed share; best linear unbiased predictions are plotted against national licensed shares and labelled an initial exploration.

The opportunity cost of licensing is evidenced through effects on years of education, the distribution of degree types (with a total variation distance summary), and the age profile of employment estimated by age-specific Poisson regressions with state-age and occupation-age FE.

The suboccupation demand story is addressed by noting it does not predict the observed sign of the employment effect and by the IV variant; spillovers are dismissed with a back-of-envelope SUTVA bias formula using the effective number of cells.

Structural parameter estimates are each benchmarked against a named external estimate (labour supply elasticity survey, training-time survey, return to schooling), and the ratio of hours to wage responses is checked against benchmark elasticities.
The proxy validation effect is expressed in standard deviations of the residualized share, and education effects are compared to well-known education interventions in magnitude.

Welfare conclusions are stated with explicit remarks on imprecision, a footnote reports what can be rejected at conventional confidence, and a bounding exercise computes how large an externality would need to be to reverse the sign.
The authors state that the tests do not exhaust sources of policy endogeneity and that they do not fully understand the origins of the identifying variation.

Limitations acknowledged include self-reported licence status, misalignment between regulatory and Census occupation definitions, CPS education excluding required training, and the static model ignoring transition costs; a footnote explains why full policy data were not collected.

The welfare formula is flagged as first-order and reliant on the envelope theorem; the authors state when a first-order approximation may be unreliable and that second-order effects would need more than labour-market data.

The authors state that estimates apply only to marginal occupations with interstate variation and are uninformative about universally licensed or never-licensed ones; Section 8 is devoted to extrapolating via WTP heterogeneity and the implied welfare differences.
Tables use three-level significance stars defined in notes; notes state the fixed effects, cluster level, sample restrictions, and cross-reference appendix variants.

Figures include maps of state policy variation for example occupations, coefficient plots with confidence bands for education categories and age profiles, and a scatter of predicted occupation effects sized by employment share. Summary statistics tables are in the appendix, numbered A.
observations.locator: Figures 1 to 4, Appendix Tables A1, A4

observations.statement: A descriptive main-text table lists example occupations with high and low interstate variance in licensed shares to show where identifying variation comes from, alongside a discussion of a characteristic marginal occupation.
The introduction previews the design, main results, and structural conclusions, includes a literature contribution paragraph, and ends with a section-by-section roadmap.

Order is model, data, empirical strategy, reduced-form results (opportunity cost first, then wages, then hours and employment), a separate threats section, structural estimation, heterogeneity, conclusion. Many checks, proofs, and data procedures are delegated to Appendices A to E.

The welfare section presents two complementary routes: a sufficient-statistics reading of the reduced-form moments, then a just-identified minimum distance structural estimation, with the text explaining when extra structure is needed.
A data availability statement gives a Zenodo DOI for code and data; supplementary data are said to be available online at the journal.
Main data are public-use CPS microdata from IPUMS with a dataset citation; the ACS is used for a self-replication; policy data were hand-collected by the authors.
No statistical software or packages are named in the main text.

gaps: No statistical software or package is named in the paper text.
R-squared and dependent-variable means are not reported in regression tables.
No IRB, preregistration, or ethics statement (secondary public data).
No formal first-stage or weak-IV statistic is reported for the IV robustness column in the main text.
Appendices A to E are online supplements not included in the text file; their content is known only from main-text references.

reading.note: All 36 pages of the published article read, including references. Online appendices (A to E, Tables A1 to A15, Figures A1 to A8) are not part of the text file and were not read; observations tagged in_appendix rely on main-text descriptions.
